newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Strong imports seen fuelling slow Taiwan recovery.
newsitem.headline: Strong imports seen fuelling slow Taiwan recovery.

text.p: Taiwan on Friday reported stronger than expected import growth in February, supporting the view of many analysts that domestic demand is replacing exports as the motor powering a gathering economic recovery.
February imports were reported at US$7.553 billion, up 8.8 percent year on year, while exports stood at US$7.759 billion, up 2.8 percent, the finance ministry said on Friday.
"From the stronger than expected import growth, we can see this recovery is pushed up mainly by domestic demand, not by external factors like exports," said Nomura Securities economist Amy Huang.
Taiwan posted a trade surplus of US$205.8 million in February, down 66.2 percent from a surplus of US$609.5 million in February 1996, the ministry said.
The February export figure was somewhat lower than the Reuters Poll average forecast of US$7.784 billion.
February imports, by contrast, were higher than predicted by the polled economists, whose average forecast was for imports of US$7.182 billion.
Economists said February's strong capital goods and agricultural and industrial material imports indicated that domestic demand was on the rise due to increasing domestic investment.

"February's capital goods and raw material imports growth showed rising domestic investment, which will strengthen our economy and export expansion thereafter," said National Securities economist Lin Kuo-yang.
Capital goods imports rose 0.7 percent from February 1996 and agricultural and industrial imports gained 8.3 percent, reversing their respective negative growth of 7.1 and 3.8 percent in January.
February's consumption goods imports surged 25.8 percent, triggered by the rallying domestic stock market, economists said.
The stock index has risen 18 percent this year, closing on Friday at 8,162.68 points, the highest level since May 1990.
"The stock market rise has made people feel richer, and this leads to higher consumption desire," said Nomura's Huang.
Economists said the stock market rally would also help lift the property market out of a prolonged slump.

But officials and economists voiced frustration at the February exports, saying a recovery in the traditionally export-driven economy was being affected by sluggish economic performance from Taiwan's main trading partners.
"Because of this weaker-than-expected economic expansion of our main trade countries/regions, our exports showed stable but slow growth," said Hsu Kuo-chung, the ministry's statistics director.
Nomura's Huang said the yen's depreciation against the dollar also has compromised Taiwan's export competitiveness.
National Securities' Lin said he was not optimistic about Taiwan's exports in the first half of this year due to slow foreign orders.
Foreign orders for Taiwan goods rose 2.03 percent to US$9.872 billion in the year to January.
"Taiwan's economy will show obvious signs of recovery after May," Hsu said.
